title: Optic Nerve Glioblastoma with Optic Chiasm Involvement: A Case Report and a Brief Literature Review
case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of painless outward protrusion of the left eye, progressive vision deterioration, limited upward gaze, and partial loss of vision in that eye. She had no other medical or family history of similar disorders.  

On ophthalmologic examination, the left eye showed exophthalmos, ptosis, optic nerve atrophy, senile macular degeneration, and vitreous destruction. Visual acuity was +2.75 diopter sphere bilaterally, and movement of the left eye was restricted.  

Ocular ultrasonography revealed a tissue‐type echoic mass measuring 1.3 cm × 1.4 cm behind the left eye. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated thinning of the macular retina and reduced retinal nerve fiber layer thickness in all quadrants of the left eye, consistent with ganglion cell axon loss.  

Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a 1.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm intraconal mass occupying most of the left orbit, with thinning and depression of the extraocular muscles.  

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits revealed a smoothly contoured retrobulbar mass extending along the left optic nerve through the prechiasmal region into the optic chiasm, measuring approximately 5.2 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.9 cm. The lesion demonstrated peripheral contrast enhancement, cystic changes, restricted diffusion on DWI (ADC value 1500 × 10^−6 mm^2/s at b = 1000 s/mm^2), and high T2 signal intensity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Optic nerve schwannoma was less likely because “Schwannomas most often show a low signal intensity on T1 weighted images and a high signal intensity in T2 weighted images, accompanied by homogeneous contrast enhancement in the MRI imaging modality.”  
2. Optic nerve sheath meningioma was less likely because “Both T1 and T2 weighted images show optic nerve sheath meningiomas as isointense to gray matter with strong postcontrast enhancement.”  
3. Optic nerve lymphoma was less likely because “In T1 weighted images, optic nerve lymphomas often seem isointense to hypointense, while, in T2 weighted images, they appear to be hypointense.”  
4. Optic nerve glioblastoma was supported by imaging features, since “the two most commonly reported MRI findings include enhancement of the tumor in the postcontrast T1 sequence and high T2 signal of the tumor. Both findings were observed in our presented case.”
